details:
**The Well-Tempered Clavier**
Bach's two books of 24 preludes and fugues each, with one pair in every major and minor key, ordered by rising chromatic steps starting from C major. The title refers to the keyboard tuning system that makes playing in all keys possible, and "clavier" is a generic term for keyboard instruments like the harpsichord and clavichord.

**Brandenburg Concertos**
Six concertos that Bach sent to Margrave Christian Ludwig of Brandenburg, essentially as a job application. No. 5 contains a long harpsichord cadenza, making it an early keyboard concerto; No. 6 replaces violins with violas da braccio and violas da gamba; and No. 3's slow movement consists only of a Phrygian half-cadence around which the soloist improvises.

**Goldberg Variations**
A set of 30 variations on a G major aria for harpsichord, with a canon in every third variation, named for harpsichordist Johann Gottlieb Goldberg and supposedly written to ease Count Keyserlingk's insomnia. The final quodlibet quotes a folk tune about cabbage and turnips driving the singer away, Wanda Landowska called Variation 25 "the black pearl," and Glenn Gould famously recorded the work twice.

**St. Matthew Passion**
Bach's oratorio setting of Christ's suffering from the Gospel of Matthew, with a libretto by Picander. A "halo" of sustained strings accompanies Jesus's words until he cries "Eli, Eli, lama sabachthani," and Felix Mendelssohn's 1829 performance of it in Berlin sparked the revival of Bach's music.

**Mass in B minor**
Bach's only complete setting of the Latin Mass, compiled late in his life from music written over decades, including a Kyrie and Gloria presented to the Dresden court after the death of Augustus the Strong. Its "Symbolum Nicenum" (Credo) is arranged symmetrically in nine parts around a passacaglia "Crucifixus," and the work ends with "Dona nobis pacem."

**Prelude in C major and Gounod's "Ave Maria"**
The first prelude of The Well-Tempered Clavier, Book I, consists of broken chords, beginning with a held C–E in the left hand under arpeggiated C major chords. Charles Gounod laid his "Ave Maria" melody over it, and some editions add an extra bar called the "Schwencke measure."

**The Musical Offering**
A collection of canons, a trio sonata, and fugues (ricercars) based on a C minor "royal theme" that Frederick the Great gave Bach during an 1747 visit to Potsdam. It includes a six-voice ricercar, the "Ricercar a 6."

**Chaconne from the Partita No. 2 in D minor**
The monumental final movement of the second of Bach's six Sonatas and Partitas for solo violin, full of difficult double stops. The collection's Italian title "Sei Solo" means "six solos" but can also be read as "you are alone," the third partita opens with an E major Preludio, and Brahms arranged the Chaconne for piano left hand.

**Cello Suites**
Six suites for unaccompanied cello, the first of which begins with an undulating G major arpeggiated prelude. They were largely neglected until Pablo Casals popularized them in the 20th century.

**Coffee Cantata**
A comic secular cantata in which the father Schlendrian tries to stop his daughter Lieschen from drinking coffee. The narrator opens by telling the audience to "be still, stop chattering."

**Sacred cantatas**
Bach wrote hundreds of cantatas, many as Thomaskantor at St. Thomas Church in Leipzig, numbered BWV 1 through about 200. Examples include "Wachet auf" (Sleepers, Awake), based on Philipp Nicolai's Lutheran hymn; "Herz und Mund und Tat und Leben," which contains "Jesu, Joy of Man's Desiring"; "Ich habe genug" ("I have enough"); and "O Ewigkeit, du Donnerwort," whose chorale "Es ist genug" (rising by whole tones) is quoted in Alban Berg's Violin Concerto.

**Toccata and Fugue in D minor**
An organ work that opens with a mordent on A, a descending flourish, and a diminished seventh chord built one note at a time. Leopold Stokowski's orchestration of it appears in Disney's Fantasia.

**Clavier-Übung ("Keyboard Practice")**
Bach's published series of keyboard collections. Part II pairs the Italian Concerto with the French Overture, which ends with an "Echo" movement exploiting the harpsichord's terraced dynamics, and the Goldberg Variations make up Part IV.

**"Air on the G String"**
An arrangement by violinist August Wilhelmj of the Air from Bach's Orchestral Suite No. 3, transposed so the first violin part can be played entirely on the G string.

**The Art of Fugue and the B-A-C-H motif**
An unfinished late collection of "Contrapunctus" movements exploring counter-fugues, double fugues, and triple fugues. Bach's name can be spelled as a four-note musical cryptogram (B-flat, A, C, B-natural in German notation), which appears in the work's final, unfinished fugue.
